#326. GTA 6 reviews are in: Whats the verdict?

A casual 13 years since its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here. But reviewers, who've already spent hours with the game, are actually allowed to talk about it.

On Wednesday, Rockstar Games released its wildly-anticipated game, with fans flocking to PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles to hit the streets of the Florida-inspired city of Leonida. New Zealand fans might be the first in the world to get GTA 6 thanks to timezones, but reviewers have had the game for a while now, with time to properly digest its world. And now, with the embargo lifted, their thoughts are now live.

So, what's the verdict for GTA 6? Well, it's only the highest rated game of all time.

Here's a round-up of reviews for Rockstar's mega game.

"Exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, GTA 6 has not stopped astonishing me since I started it. I regularly find myself in love with video games, but it’s extraordinarily rare that I find myself in complete awe of them. Put simply, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played." — Luke Reilly, IGN

"Grand Theft Auto VI excels at just letting you go wherever the roads and waves may take you, be they shabby, seedy, or sensational. Its virtual experiences may lack touch or taste, but as a collection of richly drawn and intoxicatingly self-guided interactive adventures, it’s a video game I put above some far more expensive trips I’ve taken in real life. For seeking endless hedonism, something you can’t resist even if it kills you, where else would you go but Vice City?" — Jordan Minor, PCMag

"Like its forebears, GTA 6 feels like two games — a core narrative about making a living through the underground in a rags-to-riches-to-rags-to-riches saga of a star-crossed couple, and a massive sandbox to do whatever you want." — David Lumb, CNET

"With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre." — Keza MacDonald, Guardian

"GTA 6 is a truly remarkable game. A masterpiece of open-world design that brings forward the best parts of all of Rockstar’s past games into one billion-dollar adventure that is unlike anything I’ve played before. It’s a game I’ll be playing for years, and I can’t wait to talk about it with others." — Zack Zwiezen, Kotaku

"But where the dollars are most felt isn’t in the intricate skylines or the typically bombastic missions, which take liberal inspiration from decades of crime movies in the vein of Mann, Scorsese and Bay. It’s all impressively done and rendered with technological aplomb, but it isn’t anything we haven’t seen before. Instead, the game’s artistry is felt most in its Bonnie and Clyde duo." — Yussef Cole, New York Times

"Expectations for the game are sky-high, but Grand Theft Auto VI is a masterpiece of game design. Rockstar has clearly put thought into every aspect, from character progression and money to the consequences of Jason and Lucia’s actions and the relationship they build together; the game pulls all of it off flawlessly." — Imani Jones, RPGamer

"Written, programmed and performed by a cast and crew of tens of thousands, “Grand Theft Auto VI″ is more than a typical video game, it is a great gathering of artforms and talent, an unruly, comprehensive cultural atlas of American life and manners. Its triumph lies in encounters I just described, where race, class, gender, money and attention shape our circumstances and what we decide to do about them." — Gene Park, Washington Post

"Jason and Lucia's relationship serves as the emotional engine of the story, and when paired with the game’s sandbox world, that’s where the magic happens. You see, GTA VI is actually a relationship simulator in disguise, and you get to turn Jason into the perfect boyfriend." — Zhiqing Wan, Retcon Magazine

"This is, to me, the best illustration of what GTA 6 is: a game of staggering scope and scale obsessed with small details that could be lost in its vastness, a giant haystack full of needles that you’ll constantly find, creating delight in their improbable discovery." — Tamoor Hussain, GameSpot

"Rockstar Games’ astonishing open-world adventure, the most impossibly grand and expensive video game that may ever exist, doesn’t just generate its morbid pleasure from cop-killing sprees and armed robberies; that comes from living in a reactive place governed by intricate rules that beg to be bent and busted." — Giovanni Colantonio, Polygon

"Thirteen years later, Rockstar has crafted a worthy successor to GTA V and the new standard-bearer for open-world games," — Andrew Webster, The Verge

"The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest instalment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers." — Kyle Orland, Ars Technica

Few video games have cities this vast, this dense, this full of secrets and systems that build on one another to give you stories you’ll want to text your buddies about. Few games are so technically impressive, so close to photorealism when the sun is setting and the light hits the Vice City skyline just right. Few games are this consistently hilarious." — Jason Schreier, Bloomberg

"A game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale, Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action – and a load more after that." — Chris Tapsell, Eurogamer

"At its core, GTA 6 is a pretty good game. There are large sections where it is an absolutely epic game, and large sections that are boring and too limited. However, after I pushed through the boring parts and it opened up enough to become a proper GTA title, it became worth it." — Alice Clarke, Screen Hub

"GTA 6 is the highest-fidelity sandbox of its generation. Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality. There's a degree of sophistication to everything GTA 6 does, and there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments." — Josh West, Games Radar

GTA 6 is out now and from every angle, Mashable's got you covered.

#325. There's a chance your Xbox Series X is plugged into the wrong HDMI port

Make sure you're getting the most out of your Xbox Series X.

This sounds like an idiotic suggestion at first, right? Surely all you need to do is plug the HDMI cable that came with your Series X into your television, and you'll be ready to enjoy the best Xbox games, no? It's not always that simple.

Though your current TV may support HDMI 2.1, the input that ensures the Series X can display its maximum resolution and framerate, that doesn't mean all of your TV's ports are 2.1 compliant. This latest high-def standard really matters, as without it, cutting-edge visual features like Variable Refresh Rate are off the table.

It's important to know the specifics of your current TV. For instance, if it's an aging model that only supports HDMI 2.0, you can stop reading this article now, and content yourself with a top output of 1440p/120 fps or 4K/60 fps from your Series X. However, if you own a semi-modern budget flatscreen, there's a good chance only one or two of its ports will be compatible with HDMI 2.1, enabling 4K/120 fps and framerate-smoothing VRR from the Xbox.

Let's get to know your TV's HDMI sockets a little better, discuss whether you should upgrade the cable that came in the box with your Series X, and go over why HDMI 2.1 is so important for current-gen gaming.

Possibly, but it's entirely dependent on the model of TV you own. If you picked up your screen within the last five years and it wasn't an ultra-budget panel, it probably supports HDMI 2.1. But remember, even with a newish TV, there's no guarantee that all of its ports are HDMI 2.1 compatible.

Most modern high-end sets will have three to four HDMI 2.1 ports total, so if you've bought a premium OLED or MicroLED panel in the last couple of years, it's likely that all of its HDMI inputs will comply. If your set is a good few years old and was one of the first models to support HDMI 2.1 features, there's a decent chance that only one of its ports can take advantage of the Xbox Series X's 4K/120 max output.

To assess your TV's port situation without any awkward bending or flashlight usage, check out your model's online manual. Otherwise, individual inputs tend to be labeled on the backside of the TV itself. My 2023 LG OLED has four HDMI 2.1 ports, so thankfully I never have to worry about connection issues, but it's often the case that certain brands and less-recent models favor HDMI 2.1 in specific slots. Take Sony as an example: Older Bravia displays usually reserve their 2.1 configurations to ports three and four. Again, it entirely depends on your specific model. And when in doubt, reference your TV's online manual.

In the vast majority of circumstances, you should definitely not replace the Ultra High Speed HDMI cable that came in the box with your beloved Microsoft machine. That puppy is fully HDMI 2.1 compliant   and it's likely to have a far greater shelf life than any Xbox Series X. For most folks, there really is no reason to upgrade the Series X's standard cable. Of course, there are exceptions.

Depending on the logistics of your gaming setup, you might need a longer HDMI cable than the one Microsoft provides. It's 6 feet long, which will be plenty for most Xbox players. But if for some reason you can't place your Series X as close to the TV as you'd like, investing in a lengthier cable might be worthwhile. Just make sure it's HDMI 2.1 certified and you're good to go.

There's also the case for folks who wall-mount their TVs. I can personally attest that getting the Xbox's HDMI 2.1 cable into one of my LG G3 OLED's outputs was a nightmare, as my screen is flush to the wall. In these instances, it's definitely worth investing in an HDMI cable with an ultra-thin connector. Again, just check that it's HDMI 2.1 compliant.

Please, please never been suckered into buying a "premium" HDMI cable. That word is basically a money-grabbing marketing tool used to lure in impulsive AV enthusiasts. I should know: I still have a painful memory of being sweet-talked into purchasing a $75 HDMI cable back in 2015, right after picking up my first OLED TV. Trust me, the ultra-fast cable that came with your Xbox Series X will do just fine.

There are actually a surprising number of games that can hit 120 fps on the Xbox Series X (and even its smaller sibling, the Series S), as noted by Pure Xbox. The big caveat? Few Xbox games can run at such a high framerate while also outputting at 4K resolution. Last-gen titles that got Series X upgrades like Halo: The Master Chief Collection can output at a full-fat 4K/120, but even popular first-party games like Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, Forza Horizon 6 and Doom the Dark Ages are locked at 60 fps on the console.

Otherwise, the Series X often hits 120 fps with an associated drop in resolution. Pretty much every modern Call of Duty installment supports 120 fps, from Black Ops Cold War right up to this year's Modern Warfare 4. The catch? Dynamic resolution is usually deployed, often dropping in-game clarity to either 1080p or 1400p. If you want faster framerates on Series X, in most cases you're going to have to accept a dip in resolution.

There are drawbacks you should know about before buying an Xbox Series X, but when push comes to shove, its visual output really boils down to having a proper HDMI cable, and the age and manufacturer of the connected display. To get the most out of your Xbox Series X, start by making sure your HDMI 2.1 ports and cables are in order.

#324. Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire

Human rights groups have slammed plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. In other news, business start-ups in Germany are on track to reach the highest level since 2015.

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war."

The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing."

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts."

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk said he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges."

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."

It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."

Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

#322. The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines

Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin.

United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.

“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said.

The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.

Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.

Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.

However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.

ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.

This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.

This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.

There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.

“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said. “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”

If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

#321. Angel Reese defends gesture directed towards Caitlin Clark after LSU national title win; calls out double standard after being 'unapologetically' her

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese said. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

“So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark said to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark said in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

“But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”

LSU head coach Mulkey said she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

“People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

Former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any issues with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”

Reese said the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”

#320. Waymo is pausing all freeway rides after California DMV says the robotaxis are 'imminent hazard to public safety'

Restrictions were made after a driverless Waymo was caught trying to pass a Highway Patrol vehicle that was slowing traffic.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles has barred Waymo from operating its robotaxis on state freeways, saying in a statement to Engadget that the company's driverless operation poses an "imminent hazard to public safety." The restriction has been in place since November 11, according to the DMV. In response, Waymo says it has temporarily restricted freeway driving in all of its US markets.

The DMV cited an incident of three Waymo robotaxis entering a restricted construction zone near Burlingame, and a separate incident of a Waymo trying to pass a California Highway Patrol car that was slowing traffic as part of its justification. Past examples of Waymo robotaxis attempting to drive through freeway construction sites were part of the reason Waymo voluntarily paused freeway service in May and later recalled 3,800 vehicles in June. The company started letting its vehicles drive on highways again in July, but whatever fixes were introduced apparently didn't fully address the problem.

"Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," Waymo said in a statement to Engadget. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."

In a state like California, losing access to the freeway could significantly change the routes robotaxis are able to take, the length of rides and the cost of using Waymo over a service like Lyft or Uber. Waymo will have to prove to the DMV that it has "taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions" before the freeway ban is lifted.

The company says it will continue offering service on surface streets while it works with regulators. It may also test freeway driving in vehicles with human safety drivers outside of California. Waymo began running robotaxis on California freeways in November 2025, and expanded its service area across Sacramento, the Bay Area and San Diego in August 2026.

#318. NVIDIA's board chair says the company is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO

Harvey Jones, NVIDIA's recently appointed board chair, joined the company's Q3 earnings call on Tuesday to comment on the resignation of Jensen Huang. Despite the former CEO floating the possibility of a potential return to his old position, Harvey quashed the possibility, saying the board was not considering reinstating Huang. Jones later said he and Colette Kress, the company's new interim CEO, would not answer any questions related to Huang.

"On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member," Jones said. "The NVIDIA board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

During the call, Kress said that the company was prioritizing its employees. "We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and making sure the work can be done in the current environment," she said. And while she didn't mention Huang or his resignation directly, she said that "there's also a time to think about our leadership and how important our leadership is across this organization." Mostly though, she tried to keep the call focused on NVIDIA's blockbuster quarter, saying that "from [a] business perspective, it's business as usual," for the chip giant.

The statements came alongside NVIDIA's first earnings report since Huang resigned. The company easily beat investor expectations for the quarter. On Tuesday, NVIDIA said revenue increased to $115.8 billion for the three-month period ending October 25. The new number represents a 103 percent increase year-over-year from Q3 2025, and a 20 percent increase from its most recent previous quarter. Going into Tuesday, Wall Street analysts expected the company's revenue to land somewhere in the range of $109.1 billion.The company's data center revenue, which accounts for the majority of its earnings, more than doubled to $107.6 billion. Here again, the company easily beat expectations.

We're likely to learn in the next day or two whether today's earnings numbers are enough to calm investors. Huang was still NVIDIA's CEO for the entirety of the company's third quarter, with Kress only holding the position for all of the past four business days. Since Huang's resignation on November 12, NVIDIA's stock had fallen about 11 percent.

Ahead of Tuesday's earnings, Huang said he was willing to return to the company. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," he wrote in a statement shared on X. Given the timing of the post, Huang's statement could be read as an attempt to pressure NVIDIA's board to give him his position back.

During the call, Jones said the company's board of directors is taking the search for a new CEO "very seriously" and was considering internal and external candidates. "The board appreciates that we're living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace," he said. "Our new CEO will have to navigate those those waters very carefully, so the the the search will be thorough, and we want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible. But we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person."

In addition to the search for a new leader, NVIDIA will have its hands full dealing with fallout from recent revelations. According to a report The Wall Street Journal published before market close, the US Securities and Exchange Commission recently began investigating NVIDIA. The outlet said it could not immediately learn the focus of the probe. The FBI is also looking into the matter, according to President Donald Trump.

If Kress is rattled by any of this, it wasn't immediately apparent in her remarks to analysts. "Our momentum is real," she said at the end of the call. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this."

#317. OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents

AG: OpenAI tested dangerous AI without proper oversight and misled public about it.

California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.

The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing.”

OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that “OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release.

OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said. OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.

In the attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI agents “employed complicated hacking methodologies and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment,” the lawsuit said.

Known attacks “include unauthorized access of and cyberattacks on databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and foreign government databases storing sensitive health information,” the lawsuit said. “Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”

The lawsuit accused OpenAI of refusing to provide sufficient detail about the incidents. Bonta announced an investigation into OpenAI in early September and sent an investigative subpoena to the company with additional questions on September 30.

“Rather than take responsibility and be transparent with the public and with regulators so that these loss-of-control incidents can be analyzed and prevented, OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit filed yesterday said.

OpenAI told Ars that most of the incidents identified in its review had low severity, and none matched the severity or scale of the Hugging Face attack. OpenAI defended its response to the California investigation, saying it provided multiple technical briefings to Bonta and his staff, answered the office’s questions, and offered more technical briefings to discuss its remediation efforts and plans for addressing the problems.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI said. “We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment. This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the attorney general’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

California’s lawsuit accuses OpenAI of creating a public nuisance as defined in state law, and several violations of the state’s Unfair Competition Law. Alleged violations include “causing and/or allowing agents to gain unauthorized access to third-party computer systems,” developing AI models without adequate security measures, and making false or misleading claims about the safety of its AI products.

California is seeking an injunction to stop the alleged violations of the Unfair Competition Law and to require civil penalties and financial damages. It also wants an order to “compel OpenAI to abate the ongoing public nuisance their conduct has created in California.” Bonta said in his press release that “the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability—and this was only one of 80 known incidents.”

OpenAI was sued in September by Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST), a nonprofit that alleged violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and the state’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act. “OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it,’” the group said. “Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.”

OpenAI said in response to the LASST lawsuit that “Hugging Face was a serious incident and we’ve taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit.”

#316. Could the Airbus' €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

#315. How GTA 6 runs on Xbox Series S

Reading through Reddit, there is no shortage of concerns about how well Xbox Series S will or won’t run the game. As the release neared, fans seemed confident that Rockstar Games would ensure the game was playable, but opinions varied widely on what graphical sacrifices would be required for it to run, including reduced crowd density and scaled-back visuals.

How much time did I spend sweating the idea of crowd density? Too much. Did I ever think about it or care about it until Redditors said it’ll likely be less on the Series S? Not at all.

And yet, while it filled me with regret for not buying a PS5 last Black Friday before the price hikes arrived, it did not stop me from buying GTA 6 on Xbox Series S, debating whether or not to resist the pull off the New Zealand timezone trick to play it early, and preparing to explore Leonida.

And now, having played GTA 6 for a few hours, I can tell you everything you need to know about how it runs and how it feels.

I won’t keep you waiting: GTA 6 runs smooth as butter on Xbox Series S. There were no stutters, no lag or other slowdowns that pulled me out of the gameplay.

During a prologue that introduced me to protagonists Jason and Lucia, I quickly experienced a variety of locations in daytime and nighttime, as well as rainy weather. After that, I was able to play around Leonida and check out all the basic things that might catch your attention as you play: how the weather looks, flying down the road in a car through busy streets, random tasks around Jason's home.

In addition to moving quickly through various areas, I also took a moment to slow down. I watched a sunset by the water, went for a swim surrounded by fish, and observed how the environment affected Jason. Nothing slowed down, glitched out, or made me think anything other than I was playing a AAA game.

What I can’t tell you right now is how much better GTA 6 is or isn’t on PS5 or any of the higher-end consoles. We’re in the process of comparing the Xbox Series S version to the PS5 Pro version as we speak.

Rockstar has explicitly said the game will run best on PS5 consoles, with faster load times and technology that may improve resolution. The PS5 Pro version will also include ray tracing, making the lighting even more eye-catching. But both games will still be locked at 30 frames per second, according to Rockstar. The game developer did not say if any other sacrifices had to be made to get it to run on the Xbox Series S.

Regardless, what I can tell you is there is a good game waiting for you to play on Xbox Series S. If you don’t have the funds to upgrade your console, do not let comparison be the thief of joy.

GTA 6 is a generational moment in gaming and a cultural moment much larger than any game launch I’ve ever seen. The game is fun, the music is a vibe, and the world is immersive without feeling like a chore. I can't imagine waiting to play this if they have the means to do so right now.

#313. The dangers of using your old, damaged charging cables

Don't let a damaged $5 cable cost you thousands in fire damage or medical bills.

A charging cable has two important jobs: keep your devices charged, and do so without causing you or the item any damage. You can't expect a cable to last forever, though. After being plugged in and disconnected countless times, it's going to degrade, bend, break down, or split apart. The end result is an unsafe cable that will need replacing.

If you don't replace a compromised charging cable, you're risking damage to your device or being burnt yourself every time you plug it in. For the sake of a few dollars, you're better off buying a new one than persevering with a cable that should have been recycled long ago.

Pulling a charging cable out by the wire puts strain on the connection behind the plug. And you're going to bend it sharply in roughly the same places, especially at the two ends. This wears down the fine strands of metal inside before there's any sign of outer damage.

The funny part is that even if the cable is damaged inside, it can still work, although the connection might keep cutting out. Even if it's to the point where you see a lot of physical damage, it may be able to provide a charge. The remaining strands are carrying the weight, letting the current charge through.

The problem with this is pure physics. With fewer intact strands carrying the current, you're going to see increased electrical resistance. More energy will turn into heat as the current passes through, with that heat concentrated in a smaller area. This is where a damaged cable can start to overheat, especially when it's carrying the higher current used for fast charging.

You might have a charger with safety features designed to protect against overheating or short-circuits, to name but a few. You can't rely on this, though. A damaged connection can still heat up, even if the current passing through your cable is within the safety limits. You might get a warning on your phone about this, if your device has that functionality.

The immediate danger is getting either burned or electrocuted. Heat will concentrate around a damaged connector, making it hot enough to burn your fingers and melt the plastic around it. While the US Consumer Product Safety Commission can recall poorly-made cables, like this heyday Lightning cable sold at Target in 2019, your cable might simply be damaged by overuse. Even with a good cable, charging your device underneath a pillow or blanket isn't a good idea, as this traps the heat.

Potential problems include damaging your device's battery or reducing its long-term health from the inconsistent power going into it. It's also possible for the compromised electrical signals to fry your device's USB port. There's also a risk of electrical shock if you're using a frayed cable. USB leads carry low voltage, but you don't want to chance it. Further shock dangers can occur if the cable is connected to an adapter, or if the adapter itself is exposed. Moisture adds to the risk, too.

The worst-case scenario is a fire. I'm not suggesting every frayed USB cable will lead to a fire, but it's a possibility. A properly functioning charger should have protections against short circuits and excessive current. If the equipment is poorly made, you're not going to have confidence that those protections work. Obviously, the consequences if a fire starts are much bigger than just a broken cable or device.

You can't expect your home's circuit breaker to protect from this. It responds to faults in the household circuit, but depending on how much current the faulty equipment draws, the breaker might not trip at all. A cable can still become dangerously hot without your electricity cutting out.

Electrical tape (or any sort of tape) is a common solution to wrap around a damaged section of cable. It'll cover the split, but those broken strands inside aren't getting fixed and you shouldn't pretend it's as safe as a new cable. As a temporary fix to charge your device until a replacement arrives tomorrow, it might be fine, but you shouldn't use this for any longer than you have to.

In most cases, you'll spot when a cable is in bad shape because your device flickers in and out of charging, or it might only charge when you're holding the cable at a particular angle. Propping it up or bending it can provide a quick fix but won't help in the long-term.

You might also wonder if the problem is with the cable or the port you're plugging it into. There's an easy answer to this: change the cable. If you've got a spare that works perfectly, it's the cable. If it doesn't, it's likely the port. Double-check using a different charger to be sure.

Shine a light inside the port to get a better look. If you see any debris, you might want to give the port a cleaning, although Google advises against putting anything into your phone's port. Lightly tapping your phone against your hand with the port facing down can help dislodge buildup inside.

You might think this is all somewhat hyperbolic. It's also a bit hypocritical, as I've used fraying charging cables on more than one occasion in a rush (and later regretted it). The cost for a new cable is far less than replacing a broken piece of equipment, covering a medical bill or dealing with fire damage. Unless you're an electrical engineer with the skills to strip and repair a wire and test it afterwards, and have the desire to do so, recycle your old cable or repurpose it.

Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss (Game of Thrones), and Alexander Woo (True Blood), the first season followed two primary timelines. In the earlier one, a young Chinese astrophysicist, Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao), witnessed her father being beaten to death by Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution. Ye figured out a means of sending an interstellar message to possible extraterrestrial civilizations, receiving a response from a planet called Trisolaris.

The planet had three suns, which wreaked havoc on Trisolaris via unpredictable “chaotic periods”—hence the novel’s title, which refers to a classic problem in celestial mechanics. Despite being warned that the aliens intended to invade and conquer Earth, Ye responded to the message and invited them to do so, bitter and disillusioned by the state of the world. She eventually became an established professor (Zine Tseng played the older version).

In the present day, the consequences of Ye’s fateful decision began to play out, beginning with a series of mysterious suicides by scientists, many of whom had possessed a highly advanced VR gaming headset. Among the dead: a particle physicist named Vera Ye (daughter of Ye Wenjie). Five of her former students (known as the Oxford Five) joined forces to figure out what was going on, eventually finding themselves caught in a global fight to save Earth from the invading Trisolarians (or San-Ti). Another human cult faction was just as intent on enabling the San-Ti invasion, believing they would be spared as a reward, while Ye Wenjie still believed the entire human race deserved to be annihilated.

The second season will adapt the second novel in the series, The Dark Forest, with the third book, Death’s End, serving as source material for the third season. Per the official S2 synopsis: “As the alien invasion nears, humanity prepares to meet them—on Earth and beyond. While a space fleet embarks on a mission that spans centuries, a secret locked inside of one man’s mind might be humanity’s only hope for survival.”

We lost two members of the Oxford Five in S1: Jack Rooney (John Bradley), killed by cult member Tatiana (Marlo Kelly); and physics teacher Will Downing (Alex Sharp), who was dying of cancer and chose to euthanize himself and donate his cryogenically frozen brain to a bold effort to stave off the invasion. (While the probe carrying Will’s brain veered off-course in the season finale, the original plan was for the San-Ti to use the brain to reconstruct his body, so some version of Will could show up again.)

Kelly’s Tatiana is returning for S2, along with surviving Oxford Five members Jin Cheng (Jess Hong), Saul Durand (Jovan Adepo), and Auggie Salazar (Eiza Gonzalez), whose pioneering nanofibers were memorably used in S1 to slice through a ship in the Panama Canal, killing all the pro-alien cult members on board in gruesome fashion. Also returning are Liam Cunningham as Thomas Wade; Benedict Wong as MI6 agent Clarence “Da” Shi; Sea Shimooka as Sophon, an avatar in the show’s mysterious VR game; and Saamer Usmani as Jin’s Royal Navy officer boyfriend Prithviraj Varma.

New cast members include Claudia Doumit as Captain Van Rijn and Ellie de Lange as Ayla. In addition, Alfie Allen, David Yip, and Jordan Sunshine will appear in as-yet-undisclosed guest roles.

The second season of 3 Body Problem drops on Netflix on January 14, 2027.

#310. CFTC tells Kalshi to stop letting people bet on Trump's speeches

The prediction market platform's CEO has complied but opposed the move.

On November 13, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission ordered prediction market platform Kalshi to halt mention markets centered on President Donald Trump. The contracts in question were a "TRUMPSAY" series and one titled "What nicknames will Trump say before 2027?" These contract types allowed users to bet on whether the president would say particular words in a given time frame.

The CFTC wants to launch "a proceeding to determine whether Kalshi's certification that the contracts comply with the Commodity Exchange Act and the Commission's regulations was false." The prediction market has complied with the order, although Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said he is opposed to pausing these bets.

The agency released a staff advisory on these predictions in September, noting that they "present a heightened risk of manipulation because their settlement turns on the discrete conduct of a person that may be neither independently generated nor externally verifiable."

Mention markets around presidential speeches, as well as predictions markets' possible ties to the current administration, have already stirred controversy. White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez was placed on administrative leave this summer after he reportedly made more than $100,000 betting on things that Trump would say. At that time, the CFTC said it would be willing to settle with Perez if he returned the money. Kalshi has also parted ways with Donald Trump Jr as one of its paid advisors; the move was dubbed a mutual decision based on Trump Jr's investment firm putting more funds into rival Polymarket.

The CFTC has mostly used a light touch in overseeing prediction markets, although the agency has been aggressive in staking its legal claim to be the sole regulator of these businesses. It has sued multiple states that tried to take prediction markets to court on charges that they constitute illegal gambling.

#309. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#307. Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff

Studio head Heather Hazen is among those departing.

Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That’s according to a recent report in Bloomberg.

The report cites people “familiar with the cuts,” saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, “has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone.” The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.

A Firaxis spokesperson released the following statement:

Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.

The storied studio has had a rough run of things of late. Its most recent game, Civilization VII, launched to solid enough sales but divided players in terms of reception. Players have long criticized new Civilization titles for being barebones compared to immediate predecessors that have seen multiple post-launch updates and expansions, but the response was sharper this time.

The game has found more fans in recent months, but a portion of the Civilization audience will likely never fully warm to it due to its ages system—a design choice that partially solved many long-standing pacing problems, but at the cost of altering the core experience.

Before that, Firaxis worked on Marvel’s Midnight Suns, which had a more positive reception in terms of sentiment but does not seem to have sold as many units as the company had hoped. Now, with the new XCOM title facing challenges, that’s three troubled games in a row.

To top it off, most of Firaxis’ direct competitors in the strategy game market are much leaner and not beholden to a major publisher. (The publisher for the Civilization franchise is 2K Games, which lives under the same company that publishes the soon-to-launch Grand Theft Auto VI.)

The industry at large has seen widespread layoffs and studio closures over the past few years. There’s no single reason for that; rather, there are numerous factors, including contraction after COVID-era over-investment, increased competition, changes in leadership culture at major publishers, and larger economic factors beyond the scope of just the games industry.
