#281. Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Thirteen years later, Rockstar has crafted a worthy successor to GTA V and the new standard-bearer for open-world games.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade.

That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.

Even more remarkable? The game was actually worth the wait.

At this point I’ve spent nearly 80 hours in Leonida, GTA VI’s fictional take on Florida. And what I’ve experienced is a game that combines the wide-open freedom offered in GTA V with the remarkable level of immersion from the studio’s 2018 release Red Dead Redemption 2, while also improving on both qualities. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. This is the GTA game the studio has been building toward for its entire existence.

Let’s start with that new premise. GTA V introduced the idea of multiple protagonists to the series, and VI takes that concept in a different direction. It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal.

Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two.

What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative.

The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet.

To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers.

The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play.

There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games.

All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops.

Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson.

But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time.

It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t.

Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive.

Despite spending more than 70 hours in the world, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience

I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out.

You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience.

Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time.

It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine.

Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI.

To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI.

For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it.

Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

#280. You'll need the latest PS5 firmware update to play GTA VI

Sony might be attempting to patch jailbreak vulnerabilities before the biggest game of the year launches.

Grand Theft Auto VI fans will have to download a new PlayStation 5 update, or they won't be able to launch the game. Sony has released new firmware for the console that's required to access the long-awaited title. It's encouraging fans on X to download and install it before the game's release at midnight on November 19, so they don't have to wait a second longer to start playing.

As IGN reports, PS5 firmware update 14.23 is 1.267GB in size and contains "security fixes to the system software." Sony didn't say why it's required to run GTA VI on the PS5. However, IGN notes that it was released just a day after a famous PS5 jailbreaker claimed they were able to successfully dump a game binary on PS5 firmware version 14.22. Presumably, that means they were able to extract and copy data from a disc or a digital version of a PS5 game. Firmware 14.23 may have patched whatever allowed them to do so.

Those planning to get the game sometime today may want to purchase and install it soon. The digital version is 212GB in size and would take more than an hour to download for those with a 1Gbps internet connection. Rockstar Games has also rolled out pre-release patches since GTA VI became available for pre-order, with the latest one being 600 MB. The patches should automatically download for those who've already preloaded the game.

Sony Interactive has issued a PS5 system software update that is required before playing Grand Theft Auto VI. Players should download this update prior to midnight on November 19 so that they're ready to play on launch day, November 19.

#279. Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review

Jason and Lucia’s crime-heavy love story fuels a wonder of digital urban simulation.

Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort.

This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple.

The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers.

But it’s the scenes between the over-the-top and somewhat repetitive action scenes that really make this Grand Theft Auto stand out. Almost every explosive gunfight or high-speed car chase is counterpointed by a sublimely dull, lightly interactive moment of mere routine existence: grilling burgers with pals by the water, playing fetch with a random dog, helping a neighbor tune up a car, or joking around over 18 holes of mini golf.

Taken together, the juxtaposition lends a sense of surreal hyperreality to the goings-on in Vice City and its environs. Each of the game’s two sides gives the other a chance to breathe, forming a series of emotional peaks and valleys that stretch across a truly gargantuan amount of detailed simulation and pure gaming content.

Grand Theft Auto VI never lets you get too settled with a budding life of crime or a budding family life. And it’s all the better for it.

A large part of why this works so well is Jason and Lucia, the dual protagonists whose relationship drives the story. While that relationship starts off a bit awkwardly—thanks chiefly to Lucia’s brief prison stint—it quickly develops into a true criminal and life partnership. Both sides of the relationship are driven by a mutual desire to move up in the criminal world and eventually settle down to a legit family life, if they can just earn enough from the next big score.

Of the two, Jason is definitely the duller partner. An ex-military meathead with a ripped body and a dull, affect-free vocal delivery, a decent chunk of Jason’s lines essentially boil down to “Yeah, sure, that’s fine.” While the game struggles to expose a bit of a tender and thoughtful side hiding underneath Jason’s cool demeanor, the writing can’t quite break through the emotionless masculine facade that Jason wears as a semi-permanent mask.

Lucia is much more interesting as a vivacious and amiable Latina eager to grab any opportunity presented to her. The game takes some time to dig into the difficulties of Lucia’s underprivileged youth and highlight her strained relationship with an unreliable mother, helping to add some important depth to her chip-on-her-shoulder journey of self-improvement. And even the boring Jason seems that much more appealing seen through the lens of Lucia’s good-natured teasing and genuine affection.

While Jason and Lucia can and do operate independently—and the game lets you change between them frequently—it’s their moments of togetherness that really stand out. There’s an easy, rom-com comfort to their time together, whether they’re discussing their future on the couch (“I feel like I haven’t done anything normal in a minute”), taking some time for quick romance (the game cuts away before things get too hot and heavy), or laying down covering fire for each other during a firefight (the lack of a co-op mode for these missions feels truly baffling).

There’s a minor relationship simulation component to the game, with a simple “heart level” that can rise or fall based on some basic decisions. Don’t expect a lot of dating-sim style drama, though; as long as you make the completely obvious choices when they’re presented, it’s hard to let the relationship fall apart. That’s a good thing, too, because this is a relationship that’s easy to root for, even when the participants are literally getting away with murder.

In true Grand Theft Auto fashion, Jason and Lucia’s particular way of chasing The American Dream is through a life of crime. Their travels through the criminal underworld start off kind of slow, as Lucia’s begging gradually compels Jason to reluctantly introduce her to the two-bit operators with which he’s found himself involved.

For the first half of the game, the pair are constantly interacting with a rogues’ gallery of new criminal acquaintances, each more over-the-top than the last, and all of them having specific needs that somehow only Jason and Lucia can fulfill. Many of the missions these small-time crooks have on offer end up feeling like the criminal equivalent of errands—drive here, take that, lose the cops, repeat.

And while a few standout characters develop complex interpersonal relationships with Jason and Lucia over multiple missions, most of these early side characters feel like one-note caricatures that can be distilled to a few tropey traits.

It isn’t until the back half of the game that the main storyline really starts to focus on what it does best: integrating Jason and Lucia into a persistent ring of professional criminals working toward bigger and bigger scores. Here, the missions build on each other, with characters going undercover, casing targets, and learning new skills that eventually come together in some truly tense and bombastic heists. These missions also do the best job of showing off the dual protagonist system, frequently shifting the perspective between Jason and Lucia to highlight their different skills and views on how things are going down.

Outside of this core plot, though, many of the missions and side stories in GTA VI make Jason and Lucia feel like side characters in their own story. I found myself beginning to tune out during some of the many missions in which one or both protagonists serve as glorified security props or overpaid getaway drivers amid other characters’ contrived turf wars. And even dozens of hours into the game, there were still missions that felt like tutorials, seemingly built around the opportunity to introduce some new simulation system or control scheme.

Through it all, the game can’t seem to totally shake the style of sophomoric humor that feels a lot less “edgy” today than it did when Grand Theft Auto III hit back in 2001 (for players who are old enough to remember that release, at least). There are countless extended bits where the entire joke seems to boil down to “Man, kinky sex is weird, isn’t it?” or “Hey look, it’s a male penis (or something that looks similar to one).” And the game seems to take particular pleasure in forcing Jason into uncomfortable situations with plenty of T&A, much to Lucia’s good-natured bemusement.

A word of warning for parents: This is a game that definitely earns a hard “M for Mature” rating and shows how standards for that rating have shifted since GTA: San Andreas earned an AO re-rating for hiding a single sex scene amid its legacy code.

There are moments where GTA VI’s satire cuts a bit deeper. I especially liked a couple of side stories that skewered buzzword-spewing crypto bros and multi-level marketing schemes with some welcome over-the-top excess. Overall, though, the game’s warmed-over one-liner takes on “wokeness” felt about as fresh as jokes about mothers-in-law and TV dinners, without much in the way of thought-provoking statements on society as a whole in 2026.

Grand Theft Auto VI has a gift for finding excuses to lure you into an expertly designed space and then throwing together a reason for why you have to shoot/punch your way out. That might sound snarky, but I actually mean it more or less sincerely; I was frequently surprised by the scenarios the writers dreamed up to turn what seemed like a routine trip to some beautiful locale into a firefight with way more armed goons than seems strictly necessary.

The moment-to-moment shooting will feel very familiar to Grand Theft Auto fans, by which I mean it’s dead simple to hide behind convenient cover and pop up to pick off relatively stupid enemies one by one with a dizzying array of available weaponry. The rare enemies that do manage to flank you seem to have incredibly bad aim, even at close range, and both Jason and Lucia can take a whole lot more punishment than the average quick-to-crumble grunt.

Driving around town is significantly more exciting—you’ll be darting between cars in heavy traffic to chase down antagonists, avoid the police, or simply get where you’re going faster. It’s still a blast to sample as many vehicles as you can, from zippy but easy-to-wreck sports cars to tank-like trucks that can plow through traffic, tiny motorbikes that can squeeze through tight spaces, and off-road vehicles that can explore off the beaten path.

Driving through the city also offers ample opportunities to get distracted from your main goals by dozens of side activities that dot the map. Even as I struggled to work through the story on deadline, I found myself getting sucked in for hours trying to master drone racing, chasing gold medals in countless mud-splattered rally races, or hunting for one of the many meditation spots hidden in out-of-the-way corners.

While most of these side activities offer money or improve character stats, some are simply there to be experienced. Completionists will have a bear of a time tracking down every single hidden collectible, rare car, robbable location, and beautiful landmark the developers have placed throughout the city. Grand Theft Auto VI seems set to be one of those games you can just load up to hang out in long after the main story missions are done.

Even with a fast vehicle, much of that “hang out” time can be spent simply crossing the game’s massive map. Getting from the depths of the wilderness in the north to the tip of the keys in the south is a six-plus-mile trip (measured at an apparently real-world-accurate scale) that can take 10 minutes to weave your way across on a good traffic day. During these cross-city treks, the tenor of the city’s architecture morphs noticeably as you pass from rich gated communities through the glitzy skyscraper-laden downtown and on to downtrodden neighborhoods, backwoods swamps, and laid-back island beach communities.

As nice as Vice City’s outdoor architecture is, GTA VI’s interiors are where the game’s developers really show off. Practically every story mission seems to introduce a new cavernous indoor space that’s fully furnished and lovingly crafted to look naturally lived-in and also utterly unlike anything you’ve seen before. And while you can’t go into every one of the thousands of buildings you pass on the streets of Vice City, you can enter a surprisingly large number, each with its own distinct layout and decorations.

Another element that makes all these spaces feel lived-in is the game’s surprisingly detailed crowd system. Grand Theft Auto VI sometimes packs over a hundred non-player characters into a single space, with no two characters looking or acting alike in size, shape, dress, or animation. Working your way through these crowds can be integral to some of the game’s missions, but even when you’re just casually exploring, it’s fun to take advantage of eavesdropping opportunities, listening in on individual conversations that build into overlapping chatter (realistically muffled through walls and over distance).

Grand Theft Auto VI’s spaces also seem specifically designed to show off the game’s incredible lighting system, which really shines on a PS5 Pro. The effect is most apparent at night, when car headlights streaming through a window or the rotating blue-and-red of a cop car can cast the entire world in an otherworldly glow.

But even in “normal” lighting conditions, I’d occasionally find myself slack-jawed at the details: a laptop screen partially reflected in a character’s glasses, the way rotating pyrotechnic laser effects played across dancers in a crowded club, the fluttering shadows cast by a leafy tree near sunset, or the finger smudges visible on your cell phone in bright sunshine.

I could go on and on about the little “attention to detail” touches that add up to a more engaging world simulation. Characters who fall in the dirt get dust on only the specific parts of their clothes that hit the ground. Older characters look distinctly wrinkly, with veins that show through their thinning skin. Fabric and hair flow naturally in the wind and as characters move. Rain beads on car roofs and drips off overhangs during a storm.

Through it all, one moment really stood out to me. As I prepared for an upcoming firefight, I had Lucia start eating some chips to buff her health. Halfway through the bag, I had her pick up a nearby soda, too. At first, Lucia held the chip bag in one hand and used the other to pick out individual chips. But once that other hand was occupied with a soda, she started shaking the bag above her head to pour the chips directly into her mouth.

When I thought about the effort that went into coding and recording that specific animation for such a highly specific edge case, I thought about the millions of man-hours that went into making Grand Theft Auto VI the ultimate expression of this kind of urban crime/life sim. It might be a long time before we see this level of focused effort on a singular interactive vision again.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#278. Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

#277. Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived

More than a decade after Grand Theft Auto V was first released, its sequel is finally launching. On November 19th, GTA VI will be available on both the PS5 and Xbox Series X / S, and it’s quite possibly the most anticipated video game launch of all time.

Part of this has to do with the success of its predecessor, as GTA V sold more than 230 million copies over the last 13 years. Some of it has to do with the sheer length of time between releases, a period that was plagued by leaks and a handful of delays that made the wait even harder for fans.

But GTA VI is now a real thing you can play, and you can also keep track of all of the important post-launch information right here. That includes our own review and interviews with the development team, as well as news on just how the game ends up resonating with players.

It took 13 years, a reported 10-figure budget, and the weight of the world’s expectations, but Grand Theft Auto VI is here. And it’s fantastic. The Verge’s Andrew Webster takes a break from the game to tell us all about life in Vice City, and why GTA VI’s approach to coffee tells us everything we need to know.

Lost in the excitement of GTA VI finally launching is the fact that Rockstar employees are in the process of voting on whether or not to unionize. Developer Nestor Uriarte explains the importance of the moment in an essay in The Guardian:

Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that. As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more.

Now that reviews have dropped for the game, it has skyrocketed to the top of Metacritic’s highest-rated list, surpassing Ocarina of Time (the original, not the remake). Of course, this could change as more reviews trickle in, but for now it’s safe to say that GTA VI was worth the long wait.

Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t just the biggest GTA game to date; it’s also the most romantic. Though the series is well known for its sordid assortment of criminal leads, GTA VI switches things up by starring a pair of thieves who also happen to fall in love after meeting while stealing a car. It’s still an open-world action game full of chaos and mayhem. But many players will also be attempting to nurture the budding relationship in between heists. The sprawling game is designed to support both audiences.

“It’s a risk,” explains Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North. “It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”

How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade.

That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.

Sony has confirmed the 1.267GB download is mandatory to play the new Grand Theft Auto when it launches at midnight tonight. As with most PlayStation firmware patches, we don’t know what it does though, beyond “some security fixes to the system software.”

Rockstar hasn’t publicly said who is playing the two leads in GTA VI, but The Game Awards’ nominee video says that Manni L. Perez has been nominated for Best Performance for her work in the game.

GTA VI earned eight nominations, the most of any title, including one for Game of the Year.

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS says.

#276. Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#275. Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details

“They are pretty confident that it’s going to last a long, long, long time…”

In the one light-day that humanity’s most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.

Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter’s moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a “commemorative phonograph record,” in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.

About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs’ overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.

“So much has been written about the contents of the record—the message in the bottle, so to speak—whereas I was more interested in the hardware, the bottle itself, because so very little is known about that,” Swanson, former chief historian for NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston and founding editor of Quest: The History of Spaceflight Quarterly, said in an interview.

With the 50th anniversaries looming for the launches of both Voyager probes, Swanson and Jon Lomberg, the design director of the Golden Record, recently set about writing Voyager’s Golden Record: An Enduring Reflection, which will be released by the University of Chicago Press in August 2027.

“There isn’t a whole lot of information, and some of the information is somewhat contradictory,” said Swanson of the existing resources and publications. “So it is kind of refreshing to look back and see what exactly went on.”

Meanwhile, the Voyagers continue to travel outward, still communicating with Earth. On November 18, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth—the distance a particle of light travels in 24 hours—giving Swanson an occasion to share details from his and Jon Lomberg’s pending book.

Within the immense scale of the Universe, Voyager 2 is barely even a block from its home. Were an intelligent species to find it today—some 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away from Earth—they might not need anything contained on the Golden Record to trace its origins back to our planet.

But that was never the intention of the Golden Record’s designers, who created the archive to last and be relevant for a much more distant encounter.

“They are pretty confident that it’s going to last a long, long, long time based on the data; the probabilities of the impacts from micrometeorites and things like that,” Swanson said.

When most people think of the Golden Record, says Swanson, what often comes to mind is not the disc itself, but its protective cover. In addition to being inscribed with the now-iconic Pulsar map of the location of our Sun as earlier flown on the Pioneer 10 and 11 probes, hieroglyphs lay out how to play the record and access the data (e.g., photos) also contained on the disc.

The cover also shields the record from possible damage, but nothing protects the protector.

“The designers recognized that the outside of the cover was going to wear down. It just would,” Swanson told collectSPACE. “Even small amounts of dust are eventually going to wear down the inscriptions to the point perhaps where they are not going to be readable.”

It is a catch-22: The instructions needed to be on the outside so whoever finds Voyager easily finds what to do. But if the hieroglyphs are damaged or are eroded away, the disc inside might forever go unplayed.

The solution may seem obvious, but it’s unclear whether the designers thought of it back then.

“It makes a whole lot of sense that they repeated the instructions on the inside of the cover, because when someone or something finds Voyager, they might only be able to make out a little bit on the outside,” said Swanson.

There were hints that this backup existed in photographs of the covers taken before the Voyager probes were launched, but they were either not clear enough or had other objects (e.g., a bag) in the way to make out what was there. It was not until Swanson found and referenced the original blueprints that he could confirm the instructions were on the inside, too.

There is another reason why the record’s designers may have felt they needed to repeat the instructions, according to Swanson.

“What’s the best way to convey the importance of those instructions? You repeat them,” he said. “You have them on the outside, and you have them on the inside.”

Initially, the Voyager Golden Record was a limited edition of just three—one to fly on each spacecraft and a flight backup.

“Later, meaning maybe a month or so after the launches, there’s correspondence indicating that NASA said to go ahead and make 10 extras,” said Swanson, noting that the count included the spare. “How they came up with that number, I am not 100 percent sure, other than maybe they were to make as many as they could based on the hardware and funding available.”

Over the years, various reports have either lowered the total number to as few as six or raised it as high as 14, for reasons unexplained. What is for certain—as Swanson also verified—is that the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Pasadena, California, retained and displays the flight spare.

Credit: collectSPACE.com/Tim Gagnon Credit: collectSPACE.com/Tim Gagnon

In the process of his research, Swanson was also able to verify that original duplicates are held today at the United Nations in New York; the US Library of Congress, NASA Headquarters, and Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC; the Johnson Space Center in Texas; the Kennedy Space Center in Florida; Langley Research Center in Virginia; Glenn Research Center in Ohio; and Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland.

“Interestingly enough, NASA Headquarters was not given one originally, so how they obtained their copy is not certain,” said Swanson. “It may be that President Carter turned his copy over to NASA HQ since records indicate that he had one. Archivists at the Carter Presidential Library and Museum confirmed that they never received a Golden Record, so Carter most likely gave it back to NASA at some point.”

In 2024, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied to a social media post, saying, “I have one,” without offering any other details. It is believed he was referring to a replica, not one of the NASA-produced duplicates.

Due to rights issues and material challenges, no complete versions have been offered for sale. The audio tracks have been collected on vinyl, CD, in playlists, and even a CD-ROM, which was produced for the visuals. Full- and smaller-size replicas of the cover have also been made.

Swanson and Lomberg are working on a full-size replica of the copper record to be released in conjunction with their book. But even that, as now planned, will not be playable.

“I think humanity is delighted that there were 10 spares made, because now we have those to study and look at, as the two that were flown are now well out of our reach,” said Swanson.

Suno has introduced image and video generation in its latest effort to expand beyond being an AI music platform. The new feature, called “Visuals,” allows users to turn Suno songs into AI-generated video clips that automatically lipsync to lyrics, or make images via prompt descriptions that can be used as thumbnails and album artwork.

Visuals is available on web, iOS, and Android. The exact layout differs across Suno’s desktop and mobile interfaces, but users will find a new Visuals tab under Create mode on each version. Web users can also access Visuals by selecting the three dot menu on a song in their library. From there, users can select which section of the track to use, up to a maximum of 15 seconds, and select a reference image to build the generated video clip.

There are three options available for the starting image reference: selecting one of the original character presets provided by Suno, uploading your own photo or artwork, or generating the image directly on Suno using descriptive prompts. The image generation capabilities also allow users to select specific aspect ratios, optimizing results for landscape or portrait modes and online platforms.

For video generation, users can select whether the reference image is used as the start or end frame, making it easier to edit the 15-second clips together. There’s a toggle to automatically lipsync vocals to the generated video, and tools for adjusting aspect ratio and clip length. Visuals also includes a dedicated video editing timeline for assembling clips into longer videos, and adding customizable song lyric text.

The H3 Move AI model is being used to power Visuals, based on H3 from MiniMax. Suno says the AI has been “optimized for our community including adding additional protections and safeguards,” which include a “suite of new text and visual filters” designed to block people from using or generating the likeness of specific artists, public figures, copyrighted works and IP. Visuals also uses its own “Visuals credits” to generate videos and images, which are distinct from the song credits used to make AI music, meaning Suno users will have additional expenses to pay in order to use this new feature.

The Visuals launch follows Suno introducing a Speech feature in October for generating spoken words and voiceovers. Adding video capabilities is another attempt to diversify the platform after Suno’s music generator attracted a number of high-profile lawsuits, though it seems some users would rather the company focus on improving those song-generating capabilities. In the YouTube video for the Visuals launch, one user says “FIX AUDIO BEFORE ADDING CRAP NOBODY ASKED FOR” — a sentiment that other commenters are echoing.

#273. As decision model use skyrockets, is customization the next frontier?

In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier.

Decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to quickly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice. They’re useful in production environments, where fast decisions can be more important than the reasoning provided by a slower and more expensive frontier model.

TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion company after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week).

However, it’s easy to make a decision model, and dozens were released in the wake of Jev. One Amazon engineer made one in a weekend, and soon every hyperscaler had its own option. On Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that his company is rolling out its decision model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, for wide use on Azure immediately.

The action is happening on both ends of the ecosystem: Sqwish, a U.K.-based AI startup behind a decision model called kettei fat, announced a $3 million pre-seed round today. Co-founders Ushnish Sengupta and Federica Freddi, who met as Cambridge grad students, had been developing small LLMs when Jev arrived on the scene, and they realized their architectures could be repurposed as a powerful decision model.

Data appears to be the key to a successful model in this category — TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch that the hardest part of building Jev was finely calibrating its judgment using statistically-adjusted synthetic data. Sqwish, too, has been working with synthetic data, but its unique offering is built-in post-training tools that use a customer’s own data to improve the model’s judgment.

“What makes us not a commodity, I think, is the fact that we are offering our customers the same power…they can keep uploading their production data, and just the same way that we trained our models, their models can also keep getting better at the tasks that they care about,” CEO Ushnish Sengupta told TechCrunch.

Attempting to rank decision models is difficult; Sqwish’s “kettei fat” model has performed well on some benchmarks, but most builders of the technology say that the real proof is in the pudding: It’s generally simple for developers to sub in one model for another and see how it does in a specific context.

“The benchmark is more of an invitation to try the model out, and then the continual tuning is the reason why they should stick to us,” Sengupta said.

The Microsoft-Decision-1.1 model is also the result of the company carefully balancing across cost, latency, intelligence and calibration. Achint Srivastava, the engineering VP who led the project, agreed that too much focus on benchmarks is a mistake.

“What we see is that ‘benchmaxed’ models fall flat under real enterprise usage very quickly,” Srivastava wrote in an email. “Our testing underscores just how challenging it is to deliver accuracy, reliability, speed and cost efficiency in a single model. Microsoft-Decision-1.1 and Jev are among the few that perform strongly across all four dimensions, even when evaluated on ‘held out’ or unseen benchmarks reflective of real use cases.”

For startups like Sqwish, competition with hyperscalers and frontier labs is an opportunity. Freddi predicts that future systems will see so-called System One intelligence, like decision models, working in concert with System Two intelligence, like frontier LLMs.

“Even in that future, System One is maybe a $10 billion, $50 billion [opportunity], and OpenAI is doing this IPO with you know $1 trillion, $2 trillion market value in mind,” she told TechCrunch. “This is all we care about; whereas for them, this is just a side project.”

#272. Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions

Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?

Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.

The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.

In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.

"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.

According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM, the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.

Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.

"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Leah Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.

This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.

Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST, echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.

However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.

"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.

DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

#271. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#270. Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off

Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.

OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations.

The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models.

Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models.
