#269. Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch

Tesla can restrict where Cybercabs drive and even block owners from reselling them.

There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet’s Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s “limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”

According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription,” a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.)

If owners do anything that Tesla deems “unauthorized or inappropriate,” the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.)

Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It says it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators, who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.

Tesla didn’t respond to a request for comment.

For years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services. Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers new services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.

In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, Internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors said it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.

But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a new feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does “ownership” mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for preinstalled hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” says Drury.

Tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the company has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service currently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

In exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the company says. The fee doesn’t cover insurance.

Cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly said owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”

It’s taken Voyager 1 almost 50 years to journey farther from Earth than light can travel in 24 hours.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours.

It’s the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet. It’s been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. That star is 17 light-years away, meaning Voyager 1 won’t pass by it for around 40,000 years, despite traveling at nearly 38,000 mph.

The light-day milestone is a remarkable feat alone, but especially so when you consider that Voyager 1 is still operational. NASA has done well to keep it functioning, and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of 1 light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

#267. Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage

After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues.

The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.

Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.

On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone, which is likely related to these ongoing issues.

Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues.

Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.

So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.

Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.

After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.

By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved.

This article was updated after publication with the status of the outages.

After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.﻿

After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.

“Our guidance ⁠does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping ​licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.

The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 ⁠H200 chips ​were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

#265. Deutsche Bank under fire after internal documents made public

A cache of internal records outlines the bank's dealings with Jeffrey Epstein, Donald Trump and Russian oligarchs. The German lender has sought to deflect criticism by claiming its bad behavior is a thing of the past.

Deutsche Bank is in damage control mode again after an international consortium of more than 200 investigative journalists published internal documents from the global lender on Tuesday under the name "Inside Deutsche Bank."

The documents, published in Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, among others, cover Deutsche Bank's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, now US President Donald Trump, and a host of Russian oligarchs.

Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked to a journalist from India and another from South Africa, the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers.

Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing was among the executives who took part in the bank's Russia strategy working group. The bank also still employs more than 160 people in Russia and generated 2025 pre-tax profits of €61 million ($67 million) there through a local subsidiary.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In all, the documents cover the past 20 years of the German lender's business dealings and raise questions about the efficacy of internal controls by showing that Deutsche Bank had repeatedly put financial interests before international sanctions compliance and anti-money laundering rules.

Other red flags raised in Tuesday's reports suggest that Deutsche Bank sought to set up tax-optimization schemes for wealthy clients, that criminal networks may have been able to move illicit cash through the institution, that it helped facilitate arms deals, that it helped companies in environmentally damaging industries and that it held funds for the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Beyond more recent negative headlines involving alleged anti-money laundering and compliance failures, Deutsche Bank has been trying to restore its public image ever since its involvement in the US subprime mortgage rate scandal helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis — a fiasco that ultimately cost the bank more than €20 billion in penalties and settlements.

When Sewing later took over in 2018, he promised to turn the institution around. Although he has made Deutsche Bank profitable once again, he did so at the cost of massive job cuts, and some compliance failings have continued.

Sewing to the German business daily Handelsblatt that some mistakes had been made under his leadership.

"When you look at the events today, you naturally ask yourself whether you could have done some things differently," he told the paper. "I am not without mistakes," he said, but added that the course he set for the bank "has always been right and remains so."

The bank's shares fell by up to 6% in Tuesday trading.

Deutsche Bank issued a statement claiming that the reports were old news and that the institution had long ago turned over a new leaf.

In an e-mailed statement to the press, Deutsche Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Alexander Wynaendts wrote, "During my tenure I haven't seen a single decision from Christian Sewing that I was not comfortable with."

A Tuesday statement from the bank described the revelations as "legacy" matters and claimed they would have no lasting negative financial impact on the institution.

Nevertheless, German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Tuesday called on Deutsche Bank to "provide full transparency regarding how it has addressed past failures and internal control deficiencies and how it will effectively prevent these in the future."

Further, Klingbeil said authorities must investigate and "take necessary action" where appropriate.

#264. Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases

Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper.

Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant.

How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so.

In a blog post, Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill.

Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands.

#263. Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

#262. Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories

MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a new social simulator powered by AI.

MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a new social simulator powered by AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge.

The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.

Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”

I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow.

Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.

Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards.

Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”

“We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.

MyMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.

“It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?

Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”

#260. Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work

Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors.

Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022.

Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.

Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April.

Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results.

#259. EU, ASEAN pursue deeper trade ties, but hurdles remain as businesses struggle with informal barriers

2027 could be a landmark year for EU–Southeast Asia trade, with several deals nearing completion. But the harder task will be to ensure that businesses actually use them.

The European Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) could be heading for a breakthrough year in 2027, when the two sides mark 50 years of diplomatic ties.

A long-awaited trade agreement with Indonesia is expected to take effect, while a deal with the Philippines is nearing completion and negotiations with Thailand and Malaysia are making progress. By the end of next year, the EU could have trade deals in place with six Southeast Asian states, up from just two today.

The anniversary could also revive the long-standing ambition of a broader trade agreement between the EU and ASEAN.

On November 17, the European Commission hosted a dialogue in Brussels to discuss trade relations with Southeast Asia, including progress on existing and pending free trade agreements (FTAs).

But attention is turning to what comes next. "Finalizing FTAs is only the beginning, not the end," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.

FTAs can reduce tariffs and remove trade restrictions, but that is of little use if businesses don't know how to use them, he added.

"Unfortunately, in many cases, this is where there is a failure. Communication and training are key," Humphrey said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Brussels, the priority should now be to tackle the less conspicuous obstacles to trade, he stressed.

Cutting customs delays, simplifying regulations, and helping smaller European businesses enter unfamiliar Southeast Asian markets will determine whether an FTA succeeds.

"European companies with little or no experience in Southeast Asia would benefit from greater on-the-ground support, particularly practical, firsthand guidance on informal business practices and the unwritten local rules," Alfred Gerstl, an associate professor at Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic, told DW.

One option is to expand the assistance offered by European chambers of commerce, trade delegations, and EU offices in Southeast Asia. This could range from helping firms find distributors to explaining local licensing requirements and how to qualify for preferential tariffs.

In Vietnam, for instance, sustained pressure from Brussels has helped improve market access for European pharmaceutical firms. In Indonesia, the EU has worked on trade facilitation while pressing Jakarta over import restrictions and halal certification requirements, said Camille Nessel, a researcher at the Universite Libre de Bruxelles.

Regular consultations with businesses on both sides could also help Brussels spot problems before they become trade disputes.

Trade policy has also acquired a geopolitical purpose in Brussels. "If trade policy is expected to reduce strategic dependencies, we are asking it to deliver on objectives that remain insufficiently defined, let alone demonstrating how to achieve them," Nessel told DW.

The EU wants to reduce its dependence on a handful of suppliers for the minerals needed for batteries and other clean technologies, while Southeast Asian producers, particularly Indonesia, want foreign investors to help develop domestic processing industries rather than merely buy raw materials.

The EU and Indonesia have already clashed over Jakarta's restrictions on nickel exports.

European investment in processing facilities, agreements on environmental standards, and greater regulatory certainty would give both sides concrete gains, said Nessel. "The real value of an FTA is not just opening a market but giving the EU the leverage to keep it open," she added.

Pasha Hsieh, Lee Kong Chian Professor of Law and Jean Monnet Chair at Singapore Management University, said Brussels should prioritize ratifying its investment protection agreements with Singapore and Vietnam.

Signed in 2018 and 2019, respectively, the agreements still require ratification by all EU member states before entering into force. "These delays underline the need to follow through on negotiated commitments," Hsieh said.

The issue is particularly relevant as the EU looks to develop investment protocols in other Southeast Asian states where investors have sometimes faced uncertainty over legal protections. Indonesia, for instance, has terminated numerous bilateral investment treaties, including agreements with the Netherlands and Spain.

A larger question is whether the EU should continue pursuing bilateral deals with Southeast Asian countries or revive its original ambition of a region-to-region agreement with ASEAN.

The EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-wide FTA in 2007 but suspended them two years later amid disagreements over wide economic disparities among ASEAN members and political concerns. Technical discussions resumed in 2017, but little has come of them.

ASEAN already has regional agreements with China and several other economies. Beijing upgraded its free trade agreement with ASEAN in October 2025.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Region-to-region frameworks extend beyond trade. Humphrey, of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, called for negotiations to begin on a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and Investment Protection Agreement.

The EU-Singapore Digital Trade Agreement, which entered into force in February 2026, offers a possible model for wider cooperation, he noted, adding that common approaches to customs procedures, supply-chain standards, and green technologies could create greater alignment with ASEAN members that are not yet ready for full FTAs.

"European businesses have long complained of operating at a disadvantage due to the lack of a region-to-region deal. It is high time that both sides elevated their ambitions and embraced the idea of working towards such an agreement," Humphrey said.

The 2027 anniversary would be a convenient deadline for agreeing on what comes next, but Gerstl warned against mistaking another round of diplomatic ceremony for progress.

"There is a risk that attention will focus almost exclusively on the 2027 summit in Singapore and that the group photo will become the defining image of the event, only for momentum to fade in the years that follow," he added.

#258. How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.

Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them.

Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them.

Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case.

In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow, an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon.

The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care.

Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors.

With Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover.

We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass

For products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example.

To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. (You can use them, too!) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool, which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass.

We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge. However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

#256. Waymo suspends freeway rides nationwide after California DMV order

Waymo robotaxis are no longer allowed to operate on California freeways after the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles restricted the Alphabet-owned company’s operations following several incidents that raised safety concerns.

California’s DMV, which regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, issued the operational restrictions on Waymo on November 11. However, the restrictions weren’t made public until Tuesday. San Francisco Business Times was the first to report the order.

The DMV confirmed the new restrictions to TechCrunch, stating that the department took action after three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame, and another separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco.

Waymo has complied and is preventing its robotaxis from accessing freeways in any of the markets it operates in, including those outside of California. Waymo currently has commercial operations in 15 U.S. cities.

The DMV said Waymo’s freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety.

“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026,” according to an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch.

The DMV said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken “effective corrective actions” to address the deficiencies.

Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher told TechCrunch the company has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate its performance.

“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Gallagher said in a statement. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”

Waymo began offering freeway rides in late 2025, a commercial milestone that has been central to its expansion in major metro areas. Freeway access allows Waymo to connect riders to airports and other destinations more efficiently, slashing travel times by avoiding slower surface streets.

That has been particularly important in the San Francisco Bay Area because Waymo’s service area stretches from the city south to Silicon Valley. Freeway access has dramatically shortened trips across the Peninsula that previously took 45 minutes or more than an hour.

In May, Waymo abruptly stopped operating on highways. The company didn’t cite a specific reason at the time, but several social media posts showed Waymo robotaxis driving through traffic cones and struggling to navigate construction zones.

Waymo robotaxis returned to freeways in July after the company said it updated the self-driving software system to improve performance around freeway construction zones.

#255. Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Also, the mobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has run into another speed bump. The company was already struggling to get its first e-bikes to customers due to a litany of supply chain headaches and the complexity of building a futuristic bike powered almost entirely by software. Now there is a new wrinkle, the company said in an email sent this week to customers, informing them that their wait just got a little longer.

Also said it identified “a few software-based issues, such as charging behavior,” affecting some of the Launch Edition versions of its TM-B bikes. As a result, it was pausing customer deliveries until it could work out a solution.

“Our team is hard at work on a firmware update to address these issues so that every TM-B owner can enjoy the full product experience we aspire to, beginning with your very first ride,” the email reads.

The issues were already popping up on the Also subreddit, where customers were reporting batteries draining overnight for no apparent reason, in some cases dropping from 70 percent to 40 percent or lower over a couple of days. Others noted that the parasitic drain would trigger a “bike issue detected” or “install battery to ride” error on the bike’s display. Trying to plug the battery in would often fail because the bike wouldn’t recognize the battery installed, they said.

Also has paused customer deliveries until it can fix the problem. The company said it had almost shipped out all of its Launch Edition bikes, after which it planned on transitioning to its Performance Edition. But now that timeline will be delayed beyond what Also previously communicated to its customers who are still waiting on their deliveries, Michele Mehl, senior PR manager at Also, says in an email to The Verge.

“The team recognizes this means a delay for customers who have already waited longer than expected, but believes it’s the right decision to ensure every TM-B delivers the full product experience we aspire to,” Mehl added. The company plans on sending another update on the delay on November 24th.

It’s been clear from the beginning that Also took on an enormous challenge when it set out to build one of the most high-tech, logistically complex e-bikes ever made. The USB-C chargeable batteries, which are available in either 538Wh or 808Wh packs, are supposed to offer up 100 miles of range. But the 240W power delivery exceeds current regulatory guidelines, forcing Also to work with standards groups to establish new safety and testing protocols.

In addition, the bike is powered by a pedal-by-wire system, which means there’s no mechanical connection between the pedaling and the movement of the bike. Instead, the rider pedals a generator motor on the crank, which replenishes the battery; a separate traction motor at the rear wheel is software-driven via a Gates Carbon belt drive.

Last month, when I asked Also President Chris Yu whether the company bit off more than it can chew with this bike, he pushed back:

I don’t look at it that way at all. If we were to revisit the design, I would do the exact same thing. The largest untapped opportunity isn’t cyclists who already tolerate the current bike experience. It’s the massive demographic of people intrigued by leaving the car behind who haven’t opted in yet. Their hesitations are consistent: fear of theft, avoiding maintenance every two months, wanting seamless navigation and audio, and needing to carry a child without having to buy three different bikes.

Solving those pain points requires a baseline of technology. Just like in automotive EVs, once you use software to personalize the ride and eliminate friction, people opt in. The majority of people attending our test rides haven’t ridden a bicycle in 10 or 15 years. Our goal wasn’t to go overboard; it was determining the minimum amount of innovation needed to create an experience as frictionless as stepping into a Tesla Model Y or Rivian R2.

#253. Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one

Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard.

As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own. While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems.

The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users.

The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.”

Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before.

As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added.

#252. SEC reportedly investigating Nvidia amid Huang exit

The Securities and Exchange Commission is opening a civil probe into Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The investigation adds to Nvidia’s stack of drama after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following news of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed.

The Commerce Department has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024 under suspicion that the company diverted some of its Nvidia chips to China, which would violate U.S. export laws.

Congress has also demanded that Huang answer questions about his affair and how it might have affected his stance that export restrictions should be loosened. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it more bluntly over the weekend, accusing Nvidia of knowingly selling powerful chips to China to “goose their revenues and their earnings.”

The news of the SEC probe also comes as Nvidia reports earnings to a market that has seen its stock fall more than 10% since Huang departed. The chipmaker reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago.

Meta’s own internal documents show how ‘Project Gryffindor’ aimed to ‘fuel’ the acquisition of teen users.

Meta’s own internal documents show how ‘Project Gryffindor’ aimed to ‘fuel’ the acquisition of teen users.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta’s initiative to make Instagram safer for schools stemmed from efforts to increase user “acquisition,” “friending,” and “invites,” according to a report from NPR. Internal documents revealed as part of a group of child safety lawsuits against Meta reference a “Project Gryffindor” — a school program that would “fuel organic and unattributed acquisition” of users. One internal presentation from November 2023 says a school program would “give teens a new reason to join / find more value in IG [Instagram].”

The internal documents suggest Meta considered more goals than just teen safety when rolling out Instagram’s School Partnership Program, which launched touting features to fast-track moderation reports from participating school districts. Meta expanded this program in September by creating dedicated channels where schools can share announcements with students and parents. It also adds school banners to profiles, as well as directories for clubs and teams.

Meta spokesperson Liza Crenshaw told NPR that its story “completely mischaracterizes a positive program that helps thousands of U.S. schools protect their students online, communicate with them safely about extracurricular activities, and easily report safety issues.” Crenshaw adds that Meta doesn’t “want Instagram to be a distraction during class.”

The November 2023 document says that Meta’s “current strategy of relying on power user teens to get less active friends onto IG may not be effective if there are full communities of teens that have not yet joined IG.” Another 2023 presentation questions whether Meta can “use school networks as a lever for acquisition,” and says that structured school data could “help improve the ability to find friends and acquaintances,” for attracting teens who “don’t think their friends are on IG.”

In 2024, Meta started automatically putting users under 18 into more restrictive teen accounts while facing global scrutiny about the safety of its platforms. It later agreed to impose age verification, time limits, and an option to turn off personalized feeds to settle claims that its platforms are addictive.

Meta didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

#249. Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice

Ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and said he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”

For the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

#248. Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

#247. Amazon and Google will together own nearly 30% of Anthropic after its IPO

Anthropic on Tuesday disclosed more details about the biggest investment agreements with major cloud providers Amazon and Google.

While we already knew that Amazon stood to make a killing on its Anthropic investments from the IPO, Anthropic revealed that Amazon’s total stake will come in at just shy of 15% (14.7% to be exact).

Even more interesting is that Amazon could have, if it wished, owned an even bigger share of the company. When Amazon invested billions in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024 (long before Claude Code took the enterprise world by storm, back in the days when Anthropic looked like it would forever be a speck in OpenAI’s shadow), the cloud giant obtained promissory notes that could convert into equity.

These notes carry conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share, depending on the year of investment. Amazon has opted to convert a chunk of them as part of the IPO into a special class of non-voting shares that will give it about 15% ownership. (The shares can receive dividends and convert to standard voting Class A shares when sold, the filing says.)

But it has also opted to hold on to billions of dollars’ worth of the notes for now. If it converted them all right now, it would own just under 24% of Anthropic (23.8% to be precise).

Google, meanwhile, will own just under 14% (13.7%), also in non-voting shares, which come from the conversion of notes, as well as the “private placement” sale of shares as part of this IPO. A group of major tech companies (AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners) have agreed to buy $26 billion worth of this non-voting stock. Google and Nvidia each agreed to buy $10 billion worth.

So while a lot of investors stand to make billions of dollars in Anthropic’s IPO, Amazon is one of the biggest winners, and that doesn’t even count what AWS stands to earn from Anthropic’s commitment to spend more than $100 billion on its cloud services over the next decade.
